title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching & KV cache cost model
header: Date: 2026-01-23 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 48 min | Location: Zoom | Recording: available
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran an Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache strategies and walked Atlas Financial through cost model estimates and trade-offs between hosted and dedicated deployment. Customer is evaluating a pilot to reduce per-token costs for chat and multi-turn retrieval assistant workloads; primary concerns: latency SLOs, cold-start throughput, and security requirements for finance data.
topics: prefix/KV cache tradeoffs and hit-rate modeling
cost model walkthrough (tokens, GPU time, KV storage)
deployment decision: hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC
next steps: benchmark pilot & security docs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, we really appreciate you making time this afternoon. Quick intros?
[00:12] Liam (CTO): Liam here, CTO at Atlas Financial. Priya and Daniel are on. We're most interested in reducing inference costs for our multi-turn support bot while keeping latency under 300ms p50.
[00:22] Carlos (SE): Awesome, thanks Liam. Today Sofia and I will walk through Redwood Optimize—specifically batching and KV/prefix cache recommendations and a simple cost model tied to your traffic profile. We'll show where the biggest wins come from.
[00:40] Priya: Sounds good; our workloads are very chat-heavy, ~70% multi-turn, around 600k tokens/day. A lot of short queries but some long context retrievals.
[00:52] Carlos: Great, that mix is exactly where caching can help. Quick note: my mic might cut out occasionally, apologies in advance.
[01:05] Sofia (Solutions): I'll share my screen — opening the Optimize cost spreadsheet and a traffic histogram.
[01:20] [screen share]
[01:22] Carlos: Ok here's our baseline: with hosted API, single-token generation is ~0.9ms/token on our benchmark model and costs X per 1k tokens. But the real cost sink is repeated prefix decoding for multi-turn threads. So two levers: batching and prefix (KV) cache.
[01:45] Liam: Can you define prefix cache for us? We've seen references to KV cache and prefix cache in docs and it's a bit fuzzy.
[01:53] Carlos: Sure — prefix cache stores the KV (key/value) state for a given conversation prefix so subsequent turns don't re-decode the entire history. It's K V cache in the runtime; we sometimes say prefix cache when it's at the conversation level. Hit rate depends on conversation similarity and TTL.
[02:12] Priya: How do you estimate hit rates? Our users often jump between topics within a session.
[02:18] Sofia: We use a hybrid: session-based TTL plus heuristics on context tokens. For your traffic we modeled conservative (25% hit), typical (45%), optimistic (65%). You can see the columns in the sheet.
[02:33] Carlos: On batching: Redwood supports continuous batching with traffic-aware latency SLOs. We showed static 8-16 batch sizes earlier, but the runtime prefers dynamic batching; you get high throughput without blowing up p90 latency.
[02:47] Daniel (Infra): If we go Dedicated, how does batch sizing change? We want predictable throughput during market open spikes.
[02:54] Carlos: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity so the runtime can increase batch windows slightly to amortize kernel startup and kernel selection. We also offer policy-driven burst queues to handle spikes without dropping SLOs.
[03:08] Maya: Important point — batching trades off some p95/p99 tail latency for lower cost. We can configure per-route latency SLOs so your high-priority flows keep tighter windows.
[03:20] Rachel (PM): Any numbers on cost delta if we enable caching vs not?
[03:25] Sofia: Yes — using your 600k tokens/day profile, conservative cache (25% hit) lowers token decoding cost by ~14%. Typical (45%) yields ~28% savings, optimistic (65%) around 38-40%. These are model-agnostic ballpark; exacts vary with sequence length and KV cache storage overhead.
[03:48] Priya: That's promising. What about storage cost for the KV cache — e.g., if we have long-running sessions?
[03:55] Carlos: KV entries are small per-token but accumulate. For your workloads we estimated storage under 20GB/day in the typical case; cost is minor relative to GPU inference but we included it in the sheet as a recurring storage line.
[04:10] Liam: Security/regulatory — can KV cache be kept in customer-managed VPC or encrypted with our KMS?
[04:18] Maya: Yes. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and on-prem options; Dedicated can be configured to use VPC peering and HSM-backed key wraps as needed. We'll share the security whitepaper.
[04:30] Priya: How does cache invalidation work? If a user updates context (e.g., adds new doc), will cache serve stale results?
[04:38] Carlos: We expose TTL and manual invalidation via API. For semantic changes you should invalidate the affected conversation prefix; we also offer heuristics to auto-invalidate on high divergence events.
[04:50] [08:12] Sofia: Jumping back to cost model — here's the per-token GPU time breakdown: decoding vs KV lookup overhead. With a 45% hit rate we estimated a net token compute reduction of ~30% and a GPU-hour savings of ~22% for your traffic mix.
[08:35] Daniel: Are these numbers tied to a specific quantization level? We run 4-bit quantized models in prod.
[08:42] Carlos: Yes the sheet assumes INT4 quantized models; if you run FP16 numbers change slightly. Quantization primarily affects kernel throughput not hit rate. We'll include an INT8/INT4 comparison as part of the follow-up.
[08:58] Liam: What about warm vs cold cache during rollouts? Say we deploy a new model, do we need to rebuild caches?
[09:06] Carlos: Model changes invalidate caches because KV layout changes. For rollouts we recommend canarying with a small percentage and warming the cache by replaying common prefixes (we can help with a warm-up script).
[09:20] Priya: How much engineering effort to integrate the cache APIs?
[09:25] Maya: SDKs include simple primitives; SEs will provide code snippets for prefix persist/restore. Typical integration is a few days of engineering work for a single-route integration.
[09:40] Rachel: Can you show an example transformation on cost when we enable dynamic batching + KV cache?
[09:46] Sofia: Sure — looking at the sheet: baseline hosted cost $X/month; with dynamic batching alone ~18% reduction; with caching alone ~28% typical; combined ~40% reduction (model and traffic dependent).
[10:05] [11:30] Liam: Who else do we need to involve internally? Our security team will want SOC2 and encryption docs; procurement will want pricing and contract templates.
[11:40] Maya: We'll send security pack, SOC2, network architecture diagrams. Also we'll provide a pilot pricing sheet and a 30-day benchmark offer for Dedicated.
[11:52] Priya: Can we run a short pilot limited to our EU region and have data residency controls?
[11:57] Maya: Yes — we can scope a region-limited Dedicated or Private pilot to meet residency. We'll note that in the next steps.
[12:10] Carlos: One more technical note — cache hit rates are highly sensitive to how you chunk user messages. Sentence/semantic chunking increases reuse. We can share a best-practices doc for prompt engineering for caching.
[12:30] Priya: That would be helpful.
[12:35] Maya: Great. I'll recap next steps now.
[12:40] [Recap and close]
[12:42] Maya: Action items: we'll send the security pack, pilot pricing, code snippets for cache API, and an INT4/FP16 comparison. Carlos will help scope the warm-up script. Liam, you'll confirm timeline and internal contacts.
[12:58] Liam: Sounds good. Appreciate the walkthrough. We'll review and circle back with questions.
[13:05] Maya: Thanks everyone.
